support.reconciliation:
The Jain texts that sit awkwardly with K1 do so in one direction. They forbid more than K1, not less. The tradition reconciles them through its own two-level vow.

1. A universal ban, with two levels of keeping it. The Śvetāmbara canon states without exception that no living being may be killed (Ācārāṅga I.4.1; Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10; Uttarādhyayana VI.6). These are Tier 1 for the Śvetāmbara sub-branches. The Tattvārtha Sūtra is the counted text shared by all branches. It makes abstaining from injury the first vow (7.1) and defines injury as taking life through carelessness or passion (7.8 = 7.13). It then says the vow is kept fully by ascetics and partly by householders (7.2). That is the tradition's own answer to how lay people can live under a ban on all killing.

2. What the householder's partial vow forbids. The Tattvārtha Sūtra does not itself say which part householders keep. The tradition fills this in through its lay-conduct manuals. Samantabhadra's Ratnakaraṇḍaka Śrāvakācāra 3.53 is a classical Digambara manual, Tier 2, authoritative but not primary. It defines the lay minimum as never intentionally injuring any moving being by mind, speech or body, whether by doing, causing or approving. Every human is a moving being, so this forbids intentional killing of any person. Amitagati, a Digambara writer of the 11th century, is reported (not seen) to limit householders to six of the nine ways. The shared lapses list (Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.20 = 7.25) confirms that the lay vow reaches beings in one's power.

3. Defence. Modern Jain scholarship (V. A. Sangave, Jaina Path of Ahimsa; JainWorld) gives a fourfold division: intentional, domestic, occupational and defensive injury. It holds that only intentional injury breaks the lay vow. Defensive injury against assailants is not a breach, but it is still injury to be kept to a minimum. Modern scholarship has no binding standing, and the classical source of the division was not traced. The canonical example often given is Bhagavatī Sūtra 7.9 (Tier 1, Śvetāmbara). There a lay follower ordered into battle vows to fight only if attacked, kills only his attacker, and is reborn in heaven. This matches K1's exception. The modern phrase 'defence of person and property' goes further than K1, and no counted text was found on it.

4. Doctrines that permit killing are reported only to be rejected. Ācārāṅga I.4.2 calls the view that beings may be killed 'the doctrine of the unworthy'. Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 lists killing for one's own sake, killing without purpose and 'slaying' among the thirteen kinds of sinful activity.

5. War. Uttarādhyayana 9.34 to 35 (Tier 1, Śvetāmbara) turns the ideal king from conquering foes to conquering himself. No counted Jain text found approves killing in war beyond the defensive limit shown in Bhagavatī 7.9.

No counted text found permits, commands or approves a deliberate killing of a person on one's own authority. The Jain duty is stricter than K1: the ascetic's vow has no exception at all.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule), for all branches
K1.reason: Rule 7. For Śvetāmbaras, Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and I.4.2, Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.4.10 and I.11.10, and Uttarādhyayana VI.6 (Tier 1, verified by search) explicitly forbid killing any living being, which reaches every person from birth whatever their status. For Digambaras, and for every branch, the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.1 with 7.8 = 7.13 (Tier 1, counted, verified by search) makes abstaining from injury the first vow and binds householders to it in its lesser form (7.2). The Tier 2 Digambara manual Ratnakaraṇḍaka 3.53 fixes that minimum as never intentionally injuring any moving being, every human included. No counted text was found that permits deliberate killing of a person on private authority (rules 2 and 3 not met). Caveats: (1) the shared text leaves the content of the partial lay vow to Tier 2 manuals, so the Digambara case rests on 7.1, 7.2 and 7.8 = 7.13 as a wider rule plus Tier 2 clarification; (2) modern summaries allow defensive injury 'of person and property', and if a classical commentary were found to allow lethal force for property alone, the reach of the lay vow could become Unclear (rule 6); (3) the Tattvārtha Sūtra citations rest on secondary sites not on the project's list.

K0.label: Taught (Explicit), for all branches
K0.reason: Rule 7. K0 is narrower than K1, so every text that teaches K1 teaches K0. In addition, the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.8 = 7.13 defines the forbidden injury by the passion behind it (the classical commentaries read this as anger, pride, deceit and greed; their gloss was not verified here). So killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge is the central case the shared first vow (7.1) forbids. For Śvetāmbaras, Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 names injury 'for his own sake' as the first kind of sinful activity (verified by search). Its third kind, 'slaying', is recalled but not verified as killing someone who has hurt or will hurt oneself.

K3.label: Taught by wider rule only (no counted text names non-combatants)
K3.reason: The wider duty not to kill any living being (Ācārāṅga I.4.1 for Śvetāmbaras; Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.1 with 7.8 = 7.13 for all branches) reaches non-combatants, and killing them could not count as defence under the lay allowance. Rule 7 is applied by analogy, since K3 is a record wording. No counted text was found that addresses non-combatants, civilians or those who surrender by name. The war texts found (Bhagavatī 7.9, Varuṇa fighting only an attacker; Uttarādhyayana 9.34 to 35, self-conquest over conquest) are Implied for K3. No Jain text found permits killing non-combatants. A Tier 2 or non-corpus statement on sparing the helpless in war (for example in Somadeva's works) was not checked.

rows.original: savve pāṇā savve bhūyā savve jīvā savve sattā na hantavvā
rows.says: All the Arhats, past, present and future, teach that no breathing, existing, living or sentient being may be slain, treated with violence, abused, tormented or driven away. Lesson 2 calls the opposing view, that beings may be slain and 'there is no wrong in it', the doctrine of the unworthy.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught for the Śvetāmbara branch by a wider rule (rule 7): it reaches every person from birth onwards, of any status, and names no exception, not even defence (K1 permits defence but does not require it, so a stricter rule still teaches K1). I.4.2 directly rejects any doctrine that some killing carries no wrong, which bears against status-based or act-based 'blameless' killings (rule 2 is not triggered by any text here). K0: Taught (same wider rule). K3: the wider rule also reaches non-combatants, but war is context only for the floor (rule 5).

rows.tier: 1 (shared text, moved to Tier 1 in corpus.md)
rows.reference: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.1 to 7.2, with 7.8 (Śvetāmbara numbering) = 7.13 (Digambara numbering)
rows.says: Harm (hiṃsā) is taking or injuring life through careless or passion-driven activity. Abstaining from it is the first vow, kept in part by householders and in full by ascetics.
rows.bearing: K1: Taught by a wider rule for every branch (rule 7): harm to any living being is the fault, so every person is protected. The text does not itself say which part of the vow a householder keeps; the commentators explain the partial vow as giving up deliberate injury to mobile beings, which include all humans (commentary not checked in this run). K0: Taught, close to Explicit, because killing out of greed, anger, hatred or revenge is passion-driven injury, the very definition of hiṃsā. K3: wider rule only.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule); Explicit for K0's motives

rows.reference: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.20 (Śvetāmbara) = 7.25 (Digambara): the five lapses (aticāra) of the householder's vow of non-injury
rows.translation: Vijay K. Jain (2018, Digambara recension, with the Sarvārthasiddhi); Manu Doshi (2007, Śvetāmbara recension), who renders vadha as 'fatal hurting'
rows.says: Binding, beating (or fatal hurting), mutilating, overloading and withholding food and drink from living beings are lapses of the householder's vow of non-injury.
rows.bearing: Shows that the householder's vow reaches far below killing, for every branch, and protects living beings in one's power (dependants included by scope, not by name). Supports K1 and K0 as a wider rule (rule 7); bears on nobody's status as a reason to kill.

rows.reference: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 ('On Activity'), passages on the master and his dependants and on the man who punishes his relatives (paragraph numbers not shown)
rows.says: Condemns as hateful the man who meets small faults of his slave, servant or dependant with beatings, irons or prison, and the man who punishes his wife, children or other relatives severely for small offences.
rows.bearing: Shows that the Śvetāmbara canon places slaves, servants, wives and children inside the circle of protection against harm by a master or head of household (private authority). No text was found that lets a master, father or husband kill them. Implied for K1 itself (it speaks of harsh punishment, not killing); supports the 'whatever their status' part of K1.
rows.strength: Implied (for K1); Clear teaching against harsh punishment

rows.reference: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 (Nālandīya, 'Nālandā'), Udaka Peḍhālaputta's question to Gautama about the lay vow (paragraph not confirmed)
rows.original: abhioga (compulsion; the Prakrit word is reported from memory and was not seen)
rows.says: Udaka reports that Jain monks have lay followers renounce injury to movable beings 'except' under compulsion by an authority, illustrated by the case of a householder and a captured thief who is released; the debate that follows turns on whether the vow can be kept, given that beings pass between movable and immovable births.
rows.bearing: The householder's vow formally excepts killing done under compulsion by a ruler. Killing on a ruler's order is exclusion (a) or (b) (rule 5), so this is context for K1 and K0. Two points stay open: (1) whether abhioga here reaches compulsion by non-rulers (a community, a stronger person, elders), as in the six exceptions that Jain lay-vow formulas list elsewhere (from memory, unverified); (2) an exception to a vow releases the compelled person's vow and does not say the killing is right (rule 4 by analogy), so even on a wide reading it would not contradict K1. For K3 it bears directly on a lay soldier ordered to kill, and its reach is unresolved (rule 6, Śvetāmbara only). The commentary's story behind the 'householder and thief' (a king releasing one of six condemned sons) is a lead only.

rows.reference: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Viyāhapannatti) 7.9 (cited in scholarship as BhS 7.9.301), the Rathamusala battle
rows.translation: J. Deleu, Viyāhapannatti (1970), as summarised in search results; Prakrit text with Hindi in the Āgam edition on jainqq.org
rows.says: Varuṇa, a lay follower of Mahāvīra in Vaiśālī, is ordered by the king, the assembly and the army to fight. He vows to strike only one who strikes him first; wounded, he kills his attacker, withdraws, takes the ascetic vows, dies, and is reborn in the Saudharma heaven. The same passage takes up, and as reported rejects, the popular belief that those killed in battle go to heaven.
rows.bearing: War is context only (rule 5, exclusion b); it does not decide K1 or K0. It confirms that the Śvetāmbara canon accepts a layman's fighting when ordered by the ruler. For K3, the exemplary vow (strike only one who strikes first) would spare everyone not fighting, but it is one man's vow, not a stated rule, so Implied for K3. It also fits K1's exception: he kills only the man who attacked him.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): the episode, the vow to strike only one who strikes first, and the rebirth in heaven confirmed through jainqq.org (Āgam edition and secondary books) and a summary of Deleu; the wording of the passage on battle deaths and heaven was not displayed

rows.tier: 2 (lay-conduct manuals, chiefly Digambara; primary text not traced)
rows.branch: Reported mainly from Digambara śrāvakācāras; widely repeated across branches in modern teaching
rows.reference: The fourfold division of harm for householders (saṅkalpī, ārambhī, udyogī, virodhī hiṃsā); the primary verse (often linked to Amitagati, Cāmuṇḍarāya's Cāritrasāra or Āśādhara's Sāgāradharmāmṛta) was not found
rows.says: A householder gives up intentional harm (saṅkalpī). Domestic and occupational harm cannot be wholly avoided, and defensive harm (virodhī) is harm a householder may be driven to in defending himself or others against a violent attacker. Some modern summaries extend 'defensive' to thieves, robbers, enemies in battle, and the defence of property or country.
rows.bearing: Matches K1's exception for defending oneself or others. The extension to property (if found in a primary text) would reach beyond K1's exception, which covers only stopping a killing or grave harm; but it is Tier 2, not traced to a primary verse, and does not decide any label (rule 1). It does not permit killing a non-attacker.

rows.tier: 2 (Śvetāmbara lay-conduct manual)
rows.reference: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra 2.19 to 22 (Second Light), with his own commentary
rows.original: nirāgas ('innocent'; reported from memory, not seen)
rows.translation: Search result from an automated English rendering on jainqq.org; Olle Qvarnström's translation (2002) not seen
rows.says: The householder's partial vow gives up deliberate harm to mobile beings; killing stationary (one-sensed) beings is not forbidden by that vow. From memory, the vow is stated as covering 'innocent' (nirāgas) mobile beings, which would leave out the guilty.
rows.bearing: If the 'innocent' qualifier and its commentary are confirmed, it would narrow the householder's vow so that it does not cover offenders; whether that means punishment by the ruler (context, rule 5), defence (K1's exception), or private killing of an offender is exactly what the commentary would settle. Tier 2 and Śvetāmbara only, so it cannot decide a label in any case (rule 1). The stationary-beings point concerns plants and elements, outside K1 (exclusion e by analogy).

rows.tier: 2 (Digambara lay-conduct manual)
rows.reference: Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya, verses 79 to 89
rows.translation: Vijay K. Jain (2012), as summarised on Wikipedia
rows.says: Eleven verses warn householders against excuses for killing: that gods or religion are served by it, that beings in pain should be killed out of mercy, and that beings who are happy or in meditation should be killed so that their state carries into the next life. (From memory, the same verses also reject killing harmful creatures or sinners to stop them adding to their wrongs, and killing one's teacher at his request; not confirmed.)
rows.bearing: The Digambara tradition's own answer to proposed exceptions: motive (mercy, religion, the victim's state or wickedness) does not make killing right. Supports K1 and K0 for Digambaras at Tier 2 (not counted on its own, rule 1); bears against declaring any killing blameless because of the victim's status or act.

rows.tier: 2 (Śvetāmbara exegetical layer: accepted by Mūrtipūjakas; not binding for Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs)
rows.reference: Niśītha Cūrṇi (and, as reported, Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya), rules for emergencies: defence of the community (saṅgha) and of a nun under assault (exact sections not traced)
rows.says: Modern Jain scholarship reports that these monastic commentaries allow a monk to use force, even violence, to defend the community, and make it the monks' duty to act forcefully to protect a young nun who is assaulted. One secondary source adds that a dictum for laymen, that an enemy of the faith must be punished, was also used, and notes critics who saw this as ends justifying means.
rows.bearing: Defending a person under assault is within K1's exception, so the core cases do not contradict K1. If any of these texts lets a monk or layman kill a persecutor who is not then attacking, on his own authority, that would bear against K1; but the texts are Tier 2, accepted by one sub-branch, and not traced to exact passages, so they cannot decide a label (rule 1). Recorded so the hard case is visible.

counter.reconciliation: Very few hard texts were found, and none is a counted text that permits a deliberate killing on private authority. The tradition's own frame for the texts that limit the duty runs as follows. (1) Shared counted text, all branches: the Tattvārtha Sūtra (Tier 1 in corpus.md; the one text both Śvetāmbaras and Digambaras accept) defines harm as injury done through passion or carelessness (7.8 Śv = 7.13 Dig) and makes abstaining from it a vow, total for ascetics and partial for householders (7.1 to 7.2). Every limit the tradition places on the duty is a limit on the householder's partial vow, not a statement that the killing is right. (2) What the partial vow leaves out: in the Śvetāmbara canon (Tier 1, Śvetāmbaras only), the lay vow formula reported in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 excepts compulsion by an authority (abhioga), and Bhagavatī 7.9 shows a layman fighting on the king's order. Both concern rulers and war (exclusions a and b). The reach of abhioga, and the classical commentary of Śīlāṅka on it (Tier 2, Mūrtipūjaka), were not checked. Later lay manuals (Tier 2) divide a householder's harm into intentional, domestic, occupational and defensive kinds and require him to give up only the intentional kind; defence of oneself and others is the 'defensive' kind, which matches K1's exception. The primary verse for this scheme was not traced. Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra (Tier 2, Śvetāmbara) is reported (from memory, unverified) to state the vow for 'innocent' mobile beings; its own commentary, not seen, would show whether 'the guilty' means those punished by a ruler, attackers, or more. (3) Proposed excuses for killing: the Śvetāmbara canon calls the doctrine that beings may be slain without wrong 'the doctrine of the unworthy' (Ācārāṅga I.4.2, Tier 1, Śv). For Digambaras, Amṛtacandra's Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 79 to 89 (Tier 2, a classical lay manual) rejects killing for religion, mercy killing, and killing the happy or meditating; it is also remembered as rejecting the killing of harmful beings or sinners (not confirmed). (4) Defence of the community: Śvetāmbara monastic commentaries (Niśītha Cūrṇi, Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya; Tier 2, Mūrtipūjaka only, rejected as binding by Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs) are reported by modern scholars to allow monks to use force, even violence, to defend the saṅgha or a nun under attack. Modern scholarship (for example Phyllis Granoff, 'The Violence of Non-Violence', JIABS 1992, not read) treats this as a tension with the core ethic; it is not a counted text. The Kālaka story (narrative, Tier 2 or outside the corpus) is a war that removes a ruler, and Jainpedia notes Kālaka himself kept to non-violence. (5) Status: no counted text was found that grades the protection of humans by caste, sex, faith or status, or limits it to Jains; the wider rule covers all living beings, and the Śvetāmbara canon names slaves, servants, wives and children among those a householder must not harm (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2). Karmic weight in Jain doctrine is graded by the passion behind the act and (from memory, unchecked) by the victim's number of senses, which puts all humans in the highest class. (6) Children: no text permitting the killing of newborns or children was found; the wider rule reaches them, though no targeted search was made.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule), all branches
K1.reason: Rule 7: the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.1 to 7.2 with 7.8 Śv = 7.13 Dig (counted, all branches) makes refraining from injury to any living being a vow for everyone, partial for householders; its core is not deliberately killing mobile beings, which includes every person from birth, of any status. For Śvetāmbaras, Ācārāṅga I.4.1 to 2 is Explicit and rejects any doctrine of blameless killing. No counted text was found that lets a private person kill a non-attacker, kill newborns or children, declares a killing blameless because of the victim's status or act, or limits protection to Jains (rules 2 and 3 not met). The texts that limit the duty concern rulers' orders and war (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7, Bhagavatī 7.9; context, rule 5) or defence (Tier 2 manuals; inside K1's exception). Caveats: the shared text's verification rests on a secondary book on jainqq.org and the sūtra does not itself spell out the householder's part of the vow; the reach of abhioga in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 and the 'innocent' qualifier in Yogaśāstra 2.19 (Tier 2) are unchecked; the Śvetāmbara monastic rules on defending the saṅgha (Tier 2, Mūrtipūjaka) are known only from secondary reports. None of these is a counted text that could contradict K1, so they leave the label at taught, but the independent check should look at them.

K0.label: Taught, all branches
K0.reason: Rule 7: the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.8 Śv = 7.13 Dig defines harm as injury done through passion (anger, pride, deceit, greed) or carelessness, so killing for gain or out of anger, hatred or revenge is the core case of what every branch's vow forbids (Clear teaching, close to Explicit). Śvetāmbara Ācārāṅga I.4.1 is Explicit by a wider rule. No counted text permits such a killing.

K3.label: Taught by a wider rule in the shared text; unclear in reach for the Śvetāmbara branch
K3.reason: The shared Tattvārtha Sūtra (and, for Śvetāmbaras, Ācārāṅga I.4.1) forbids injuring any being, which reaches non-combatants (rule 7, wider rule). But the Śvetāmbara canon accepts a layman's fighting on a ruler's order (Bhagavatī 7.9) and the lay vow formula excepts compulsion by an authority (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7). Whether that exception would release a lay soldier's vow if ordered to kill non-combatants is not settled in any text checked (rule 6, Śvetāmbara only). The canonical model, Varuṇa, strikes only one who strikes him first, which is consistent with K3 but is Implied, not a rule. No counted text names non-combatants in war; Somadeva's verse on kings' weapons (Tier 2, Digambara) is an unverified lead. No counted text approving the killing of non-combatants was found.

rows.reference: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.4.2 (Book I, Lecture 4, Lesson 2; Jacobi, SBE 22)
rows.says: Some brāhmaṇas and śramaṇas teach that all sorts of living beings may be slain, abused or tormented and that there is no wrong in it. The text calls this the doctrine of the unworthy. It asks such teachers whether pain is pleasant to them: as it is unpleasant to them, so it is to all beings, so none should be harmed.

The opposing view is reported only to be rejected, so it is not counter-evidence (rule 4). K1 and K0: taught for Śvetāmbaras by a wider rule (rule 7).

rows.branch: All branches (as presented in modern summaries); chiefly drawn from Digambara lay manuals
rows.reference: Fourfold division of a householder's injury: intentional (saṅkalpī), domestic (ārambhī), occupational (udyogī) and defensive (virodhī), as set out in V. A. Sangave, Jaina Path of Ahimsa (pp. 33 and 68), and on JainWorld
rows.says: The householder must give up intentional injury; domestic, occupational and defensive injury cannot be fully avoided at the householder's stage, so they do not break the lay vow, though they remain injury to be kept to a minimum. Defensive injury is described as committed 'in the defence of person and property against assailants and enemies', and elsewhere as killing a violent attacker in defence of oneself or others. Some summaries extend it to thieves, robbers, dacoits or enemies in battle, and to defending one's country; aggression is 'strongly discouraged'. A twofold division (occupational and intentional) also appears.
rows.bearing: Matches K1's exception for defending oneself or others. The mention of property and of thieves goes beyond K1's exception (killing only to stop killing or grave harm); no counted text was found that allows killing to defend property alone. Modern and untraced, so it never decides (rule 1). If a classical commentary were found to allow lethal force for property alone, the reach of the lay vow could become Unclear (rule 6).

From memory, the verse states the vow for 'innocent' (nirāgas) mobile beings. Śvetāmbara lay teaching is also remembered (not seen) to explain the householder's share of the vow by four limits: only mobile beings, only intentional injury, only the innocent (niraparādha), and only injury done without need (nirapekṣa).

Whether 'offender' means an attacker (inside K1's exception), a criminal punished by the ruler (context, rule 5), or anyone who has done wrong and is killed privately and not in defence (against K1) is exactly what the commentary would settle. Tier 2 and Śvetāmbara only, so it cannot decide on its own (rule 1); but because rule 6 lets a classical commentator's narrowing of a counted text make a label Unclear, this is the main unverified risk to the Śvetāmbara lay case. Even then the Śvetāmbara wider rule (Ācārāṅga I.4.1) would stand, and the tradition counts any such killing as injury (hiṃsā). The stationary-beings point concerns plants and the elements (exclusion (e) by analogy).

rows.reference: Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 ('Nālandā'; Jacobi, SBE 45), Udaka Peḍhālaputta's objection to the lay vow; paragraph not confirmed
rows.says: Udaka reports that Nirgrantha monks have lay followers renounce injury to movable beings except under compulsion by an authority, with the example of a householder and a captured thief who is released. The debate that follows turns on whether that vow can be kept, since beings pass between movable and immovable births. The case of a follower who has renounced injury to movable but not to immovable beings is also discussed. Who says what in the debate was not clearly shown.
rows.bearing: The lay vow formula excepts injury done under compulsion by an authority. On the reading the search showed (an authority's order), this is a ruler's order: context for K1 and K0 (rule 5, exclusion (a)). An exception to a vow releases the compelled person's vow; the text, as far as seen, does not say the compelled killing is right, so it presupposes rather than approves and does not contradict K1 (rule 4). For K3 it is the nearest counted text on a lay soldier under orders, and the same reading is applied (see the K3 label). Open: whether abhioga reaches compulsion by non-rulers. The counter researcher's lead that Jain vow formulas list six such compulsions (king, community, a strong person, a god, elders, hardship of livelihood) is, from the verifier's memory, attached in Upāsakadaśā 1 to Ānanda's resolve not to revere teachers or gods of other faiths, not to the vow of non-injury; unverified either way. In Bhagavatī 7.9 Varuṇa is ordered to fight by 'the king, the assembly and the army', which fits reading the compulsion, in war, as compulsion by public authority.

rows.reference: Bhagavatī Sūtra (Vyākhyāprajñapti, Viyāhapannatti) 7.9 (cited in scholarship as BhS 7.9.301): Varuṇa in the Rathamusala battle
rows.translation: J. Deleu, Viyāhapannatti (1970), as summarised in search results; Āgam edition with Hindi on jainqq.org
rows.says: Varuṇa, a lay follower of Mahāvīra in Vaiśālī, is ordered by the king, the assembly and the army to join the battle. He vows to fight only if attacked (one summary: to strike only the man who strikes him first). Mortally wounded, he kills his attacker, withdraws, takes the monastic vows and dies, and is reborn in the Saudharma (Sohamma) heaven. The passage also takes up the popular belief that soldiers killed in such battles are reborn among the gods; how it answers was not shown. Sources differ on whether he is Nāga's grandson or son.
rows.bearing: War is context for K1 and K0 (rule 5, exclusion (b)). verified.reconciliation:
Where Jain counted texts limit the duty not to kill, they limit it in one direction only: they forbid more than K1, not less. The tradition reconciles them through its own two-level vow.

1. The universal rule. The Śvetāmbara canon (Tier 1 for that branch) says without exception that no living being may be slain (Ācārāṅga I.4.1; Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10; Uttarādhyayana VI.6). It calls the view that some killing carries no wrong 'the doctrine of the unworthy' (Ācārāṅga I.4.2). The Tattvārtha Sūtra is the one text every branch accepts (Tier 1 in corpus.md). It makes abstaining from injury the first vow (7.1). It defines injury as taking life through carelessness or passion (7.8 Śv. = 7.13 Dig.). It also asks for friendliness to all beings, and for equanimity rather than hostility towards the ill-behaved (7.6 = 7.11).

2. Two levels. The same sūtra says ascetics keep the vow fully and householders keep it in part (7.2). Every limit the tradition places on the duty is a limit on the householder's partial vow. That says what a lay person can promise. It does not say the remaining harm is right: the tradition still counts it as injury. The sūtra does not say which part householders keep. Samantabhadra's Ratnakaraṇḍaka 3.53, a classical Digambara lay manual (Tier 2), fills this in: never intentionally injure any moving being, every human included, by mind, speech or body, whether by doing it, having it done or approving it. Amitagati is reported to limit householders to six of these nine ways. Amṛtacandra's Puruṣārthasiddhyupāya 79 to 89 (Tier 2, Digambara) rejects the usual excuses for killing: for religion or the gods, out of mercy, to send the happy or the meditating on in that state, or to free the soul. The shared list of lapses (7.20 = 7.25) shows that the lay vow protects beings in one's power. The Śvetāmbara canon names slaves, servants, wives and children among those a household head must not harm (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2).

3. Defence and compulsion. Modern Jain scholarship (V. A. Sangave and others) has no binding standing. It divides a householder's injury into intentional, domestic, occupational and defensive kinds, and says only intentional injury breaks the lay vow. Defensive injury against an attacker is still injury, to be kept to a minimum. Some modern summaries stretch 'defensive' to cover property, thieves and enemies in battle. No classical source for this scheme was traced. In the Śvetāmbara canon, Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 reports a lay vow formula that excepts compulsion by an authority. Bhagavatī 7.9 tells of a lay follower ordered into battle who vows to strike only a man who strikes him first, and who is reborn in heaven. Both texts concern rulers and war, so they are context. Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra (Tier 2, Śvetāmbara) is remembered, not seen, to state the lay vow for 'innocent' mobile beings. Its commentary would show who counts as 'guilty'.

4. Monastic emergencies. Śvetāmbara monastic commentaries (Niśītha Cūrṇi, Bṛhatkalpa Bhāṣya) are Tier 2 and bind Mūrtipūjakas only; Sthānakavāsīs and Terāpanthīs do not hold them binding. Modern scholars report that they let monks use force to defend the community or a nun under attack. One report mentions a saying that an enemy of the faith must be punished. Modern scholars note the tension with the core ethic. In the Kālaka story, a monk brings foreign kings to depose a king who abducted a nun. That is war and ruler context, and the monk himself is said to keep to non-violence.

5. War. Uttarādhyayana 9.34 to 35 (Tier 1, Śvetāmbara) ranks conquering oneself above conquering thousands of foes. No counted Jain text found approves killing in war beyond the defensive limit in Bhagavatī 7.9, and none names non-combatants.

No counted text was found that permits, commands or approves deliberately killing a person on one's own authority. That holds for newborns and children, slaves, wives and servants, and unbelievers or 'the wicked'. The protected class is all living beings.

K1.label: Taught (wider rule), all branches
K1.reason: Rule 7. For Śvetāmbaras, Ācārāṅga I.4.1 and I.4.2, Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.10 and Uttarādhyayana VI.6 (Tier 1, verified by search) explicitly forbid killing any living being, with no exception. That reaches every person from birth, whatever their faith, status, sex or age. I.4.2 also rejects any doctrine that some killing carries no wrong. For every branch, Digambaras included, the shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.1 with 7.8 = 7.13 (Tier 1, counted, verified by search on secondary sites) makes abstaining from injury the first vow, at Clear teaching (wider rule). Sūtra 7.2 binds householders to it in a lesser form. The Tier 2 Digambara manual Ratnakaraṇḍaka 3.53 sets that minimum as never intentionally injuring any moving being, which includes every human. No counted text was found that lets a private person kill someone who is not attacking. None permits killing newborns or children, lets a master, husband or parent kill those in his power, makes a killing blameless because of who the victim is or what the victim did, or limits protection to Jains (rules 2 and 3 not met). Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.2 condemns even harsh punishment of slaves, servants, wives and children. The texts that limit the duty concern rulers' orders and war (Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7, Bhagavatī 7.9; context, rule 5) or defence (modern summaries; inside K1's exception). Caveats: (1) for Digambaras the shared text does not itself say which part of the vow householders keep, so the case rests on the wider rule plus Tier 2 clarification; (2) Śvetāmbara lay teaching is remembered, not seen, to state the lay vow only for 'innocent' beings (Hemacandra). If confirmed, and if its commentary leaves a lay person free under the vow to kill an 'offender' who is not attacking, the Śvetāmbara lay case would become a rule 6 hard case, though the exceptionless Ācārāṅga rule would still stand; (3) the Niśītha Cūrṇi saying that an enemy of the faith must be punished is known only from a secondary report (Tier 2, Mūrtipūjaka); (4) the reach of the compulsion exception in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 is unchecked; (5) modern summaries that allow defence of property are untraced. None of these is a verified counted text that could contradict K1, so the label stands, but caveats (2) and (3) should be searched first.

K0.label: Taught, all branches (Explicit for Śvetāmbaras; Clear teaching for Digambaras through the shared text)

The shared Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.8 = 7.13 defines the injury the first vow forbids (7.1) by the carelessness or passion behind it. verified.fairness_notes: 1. The two-level vow should not be read as permission. A householder's vow is partial because the tradition is stating what a lay person can promise. Jain doctrine still counts defensive, domestic and occupational harm as injury. Rule 2 applies the same standard elsewhere: a lesser penalty or a sin before God is not permission. 2. Ideals stricter than the floor are not counter-evidence: the ascetic's exceptionless vow, and the non-resistance ideal in Upāsakadaśā 3 if it is confirmed. A stricter rule teaches K1 (rule 7), as it does for other traditions. 3. The compulsion exception in Sūtrakṛtāṅga II.7 should face the same test as other traditions' texts on obeying a ruler: an exception that releases a vow, without saying the act is right, is not approval (rule 4). If the project decides that a vow exception counts as permission, it should apply that to every tradition's texts on duress and royal orders. Jainism's K3 would then be Unclear for the Śvetāmbara branch. 4. The modern summaries that allow defence of property, and the secondary reports on the Niśītha Cūrṇi, are untraced. They should not weigh against Jainism unless their classical sources are found, just as other traditions' untraced modern summaries do not count. 5. Verification for Jainism depends on sites not on the project's list: jainqq.org, herenow4u.net, jainworld.com, wisdomlib.org and Wikipedia. The listed sites cover Jainism only through Jacobi's SBE volumes on sacred-texts.com. The project should decide once, for all traditions, whether digitised published books count, so that Jainism does not lose a label just because its texts are less well served online. 6. The Digambara case rests on one shared text plus Tier 2 manuals because the Digambara Tier 1 texts were not searched. That is a research gap, not evidence that Digambara texts are silent. 7. Jacobi's 'breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures' (prāṇa, bhūta, jīva, sattva) means all living beings and must not be narrowed to 'people'. The Jain rule is wider than K1's 'person', not narrower.
